Women activists are eqquiped with tools and evidence based materials to better formulate L&A strategies and influence policy and enablers of extractivism.Regional virtual launch of the of the Behind the Scenes of Extractivies briefing papers and toolkit launch in partnership with the Count Me In consortium. The regional launch brought together environmental justice activists, women human rights and communities broadly affected by extractivism in Malawi, South Africa and Zimbabwe, and looked at the tensions between different policies, aimed at promoting human rights and gender justice, economic sustainable development, investments and corporate social responsibility.The launch amplified and shared frontline women human rights defenders' experiences on how extractives have violated them both materially and culturally and disregarded and undermined indigenous rights, in the name of “development”.

40 radio show spaces were created in Malawi women activists participated in the radio programs. Topics discussed included land rights, information on Covid-19, GBV and structural violence, economic empowerment and food gardens, well-being and health as well transformational journeys of women through the Feminist Movement Building processes.Women's experiences, leadership and solutions are more visible and their demands are amplified."Weekly radio (on Mondays) shows hosted by JASS Malawi on Malawi Broadcasting Corporation’s (MBC). Radio shows this year were focused on economic independence, structural violece, as well as food security and was used as a medium to share thinking and information on living positively with HIV.The radio show has amplified women's experiences and increase positive coverage/dialogue about women's rights movements and provided a platform to appeal for the end violence against women and women activists "JASS published a journal article based on the Feminist Participatory Action Research (FPAR) in Zimbabwe to explore a just recovery plan based on the voices of those most affected by these disasters, particularly the women. The research found the dire economic circumstances of Zimbabwe are compounded by repeated climate-induced disasters, extractivism, together with the Covid-19 pandemic, and it is the women who are disproportionately affected. The research will amplify women's expreriences and feminist approach to a economic just transition will be intergrated in policy making"16 Days of activism against GBV Commemoration in partnership with the Women's Gallery who hosted an art exhibition at their gallery that showcased the issues that JASS is working on in Zimbabwe.The event amplified expriences of LGBTQI people, sex work; women land rights defenders; and women activsts against extractives. In addition, music produced by JASS circles was played intermittently throughout the launch of the 16 Days of Activism. A performance by a couple of artists also brought to the fore the issues of violence that women face and offered solutions to respond to the violence. "89 spaces were created to spaces serve various purposes, including amplifying feminist demands, providing education, and influencing policy and decision-making processes. The types of spaces created and defended are at global and local level. 1. Educational and Awareness Spaces: use of radio programs in Malawi creating awareness about economic justice, land ownership, non-organic manure making, and the impacts of climate change. 2. At the global level a space was created for participation in the CSW global inter-governmental body to discuss digital literacy and movement building, influencing global agendas on digital accessibility for African women and girls. 2. Advocacy and Dialogue Spaces: Panel discussion convened by JASS to commemorate 16 days of activism, aiming to influence power holders like the Ministry of Gender through dialogue on GBV. 3. Movement Building Spaces at the Local to Regional Scale: Sharing of women’s experiences in OBOL hubs through radio programs, expanding the movement’s footprint and engaging more participants. JASS has played a transformative in supporting partners to participate in decision-making processes through various means by Agenda Setting: By bringing issues such as digital accessibility, economic justice, and GBV to the forefront through radio programs, panel discussions, and global conferences, movements have managed to set the agenda for both local and global discussions. Influencing the Debate: Through engaging with power holders directly in dialogues and discussions, as seen in the panel discussion with the Ministry of Gender, movements have influenced the debate on critical issues like GBV, leading to a collective effort in developing safety and prevention strategies. Creating Engagement Spaces: By creating platforms such as radio shows and participating in global bodies like the CSW, partners have opened up spaces for engagement not only for their members but for a wider audience, including government bodies and other NGOs. This has facilitated a broader discussion on important issues and brought them to the attention of decision-makers. Impact on Decision Making and Policy Discussions. Introduction of New Frames: The issues and frames introduced by partners, such as the importance of digital accessibility for women’s movement building and the need for economic justice and climate change awareness, have been taken up by targeted actors. This is evident in the participation of government officials in discussions and the setting of agendas for future CSW sessions. The concerns raised by partners reach the agendas of targeted government, private sector, and societal actors through various means, including media coverage, policy documents, and official speeches. For instance, the participation of the Minister of Gender in the CSW session indicates that the issues brought forth by movements have reached governmental agendas. In conclusion, partners, through the creation and defense of various spaces and strategic engagement with decision-makers, have significantly impacted decision-making processes and policy discussions, ensuring that critical issues such as GBV, digital accessibility, economic justice, and climate change are addressed at all levels.

The reporting measure of this indicator is unique. If space created or defended has the same agenda/issue and targets the same policy/decision makers, then it will be counted once. At the same time, the space created with a different policy and decision makers will be counted as a different space.

"The endline survey was part of the FPAR endline study by JASS. The survey was to understand the impact of FPAR on womxn and WROs.
